evidence.raw_text: Mind the Location Leakage in LEO Direct-to-Cell Satellite Networks

Leveraging direct-to-cell (DTC) satellites in low-earth orbits (LEO) to directly provide communication services for terrestrial cellphones is gaining popularity in recent years. However, the unique characteristics of the wireless medium in space-ground communication, combined with the dynamic behavior of LEO satellites, raise a new privacy leakage risk that an adversary eavesdropping on DTC broadcasts could steal the physical locations of active users. In this paper, we investigate new techniques to analyze the location leakage risks in emerging LEO direct-to-cell satellite networks (DCSN). We present DCATOR 1 , a novel location leakage analyzer which continuously monitors DTC signaling messages in broadcast channels, extracts various location clues and combines them with the time-varying satellite trajectories to infer the physical locations of active users. We use DCATOR to analyze the consequences if an adversary is able to continuously monitor and process broadcast DTC signaling to deduce the locations of other users within the same satellite coverage area, in three representative DCSNs: (i) the operational Iridium; (ii) the developing Starlink DTC; and (iii) a DCSN based on the latest 3GPP NTN standards. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the existence of location leakages in real DCSNs, and in the worst case an adversary can precisely track the locations of other users within hundreds of meters. Finally, we propose privacy-enhancing countermeasures for DCSNs. 1064 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

In this paper, we investigate new techniques to analyze the location leakage risks in emerging LEO direct-to-cell satellite networks (DCSN). We present DCATOR1, a novel location leakage analyzer which continuously monitors DTC signaling messages in broadcast channels, extracts various location clues and combines them with the time-varying satellite trajectories to infer the physical locations of active users. We use DC ATOR to analyze the consequences if an adversary is able to continuously monitor and process broadcast DTC signaling to deduce the locations of other users within the same satellite coverage area, in three representative DCSNs: (i) the operational Iridium; (ii) the developing Starlink DTC; and (iii) a DCSN based on the latest 3GPP NTN standards. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the existence of location leakages in real DCSNs, and in the worst case an adversary can precisely track the locations of other users within hundreds of meters. Finally, we propose privacy-enhancing countermeasures for DCSNs. 1. Introduction With the rapid deployment of emerging low-earth orbit (LEO) mega-constellations, satellite operators such as Iridium [1], SpaceX [2] and AST SpaceMobile [3] are actively construct- ing their direct-to-cell satellite networks (DCSN) to provide communication services for terrestrial cellphones, especially for those in remote areas (e.g., forests, oceans, deserts). These direct-to-cell (DTC) satellites, as the name suggests, can directly communicate with customized or commercial-of-the- shelf (COTS) mobile cellphones to enable ubiquitous short message, telephony and Internet access, without relying on dedicated dish-like antennas like residential users ( e.g., [4], [5]). In this paper, we refer to these cellphones that can communicate straightforwardly with satellites as satphones or user equipments (UE) interchangeably. A user's physical location is a key privacy element of personal data protected under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [6]. Once the location information leaks, 1. Since the 2G era of traditional wireless and mobile networks, because the use of wireless media for communication increases the risk of privacy leakage, extensive efforts focusing on location leakage analysis and corresponding mitigation have been proposed by the S&P community ( e.g., [13]-[21]). However, different from traditional wireless and mobile networks, emerging DCSNs have several new characteristics such as: the core network infrastructure ( i.e., a network of LEO satellites) is constantly moving at a high speed relative to the earth's surface, and the spot beam coverage of a satellite is much wider than a traditional cellular base station. Such new characteristics diminish the effectiveness of existing location leakage analysis methods, which were originally designed for conventional cellular networks. For example, previous studies that analyzed whether a cellphone is presented in a cell/city [13]-[18] or inferred UEs' precise locations [19]-[21] in cellular networks, can not be directly applied to DCSNs for several reasons. On the one hand, because the coverage area of a satellite spot beam is typically large ( e.g., the diameter is about 400km for Iridium [22] and 24km for Starlink [23]), identifying the presence of a satphone within a cell or city does not provide sufficient precision for localization. On the other hand, for precise location inference, existing methods need to sniff the uplink signals launched by cellphones. For 4G Long Term Evolution (LTE) and 5G New Radio (NR), sniffers should be deployed near the target to catch high-quality uplink signals due to the low uplink transmit power of COTS phones. However, in DCSNs, even when both the sniffer and the target are within the same spot beam, monitoring uplink signals over long distances remains challenging, thereby limiting the range of effective detection and analysis. In addition, few works have specifically studied satphone location leakage in the context of DCSNs. A recent effort RECORD [24] proposes a paging-based method to determine the possible ranges of UE location. It obtains multiple ranges via observing Paging messages at different time and intersects the ranges to infer the region of UE. However, RECORD requires a long observation time to narrow down the potential region, and its localization accuracy remains at the kilometer scale. For example, it takes approximately 2.3 hours to reduce the radius of region to 11 km, while shrinking the radius to 4 km requires 16 hours. Facing emerging DCSNs, this paper investigates more accurate and efficient approaches to analyze new privacy risks of location leakage raised by the coexistence of wireless 1064 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00140 medium in space-ground communication and the dynamic nature of LEO satellites. We present DCATOR, a new location leakage analyzer that can analyze the consequences if an ad- versary can cleverly sniff DTC broadcast signaling messages to deduce the locations of other users in the same satellite coverage. In principle, DCATOR leverages a key insight that: while the location information might not be directly embedded in wireless signaling messages, user locations can be inferred by several location clues ( e.g., propagation delay and Doppler shift) hidden in broadcast channels. For example, an adversary can calculate the distance between a satphone and the connected satellite based on the propagation delay. As satellites move, propagation delay and Doppler shift vary continuously and should be periodically broadcast. Thus, the adversary can collect multiple location-related signaling messages in a short duration and track the time- varying distances between the satphone and the connected satellite. As one distance implicitly determines one location range of the satphone ( e.g., a spherical surface centered on a certain satellite) and satellite trajectories are predictable, it is feasible to find a point that satisfies all the range constraints to determine the precise location of the target satphone. However, realizing the above ideas in real DCSNs requires to address several practical challenges: (i) when a satphone stays in the idle status, it does not exchange location-related signaling messages with the satellite, and thus no location clues can be monitored; (ii) when multiple satphones connect to the same satellite, it is challenging to exactly identify the signaling messages of the target satphone; (iii) due to the high dynamics and long communication distance of satellites, the location-related information extracted from the broadcast signaling may experience large systematic error in DCSNs. DCATOR tackles these practical challenges by the follow- ing wisdom. First, to monitor the location-related signaling messages from idle users, DCATOR makes ghost calls to the target satphones and forces them into active state. Second, to extract the signaling messages belonging to the target satphone, DCATOR compares the frequency of ghost calls to the frequency of specific signaling messages, and identifies the one with similar frequency. Finally, DCATOR formulates the location inference problem as an optimization problem and seeks the location that minimizes the inference error. We implement DC ATOR prototypes2 and build several testbeds to analyze the location leakage across three represen- tative direct-to-cell standards: GSM extension, reusing LTE protocols and 3GPP NTN. For GSM extension protocols, we evaluate DCATOR in a commercial DCSN, Iridium. For LTE and NTN protocols, our testbeds exploit public constellation information of Starlink to mimic the LEO movements and emulate real protocol behaviors. Extensive experiments show that DCATOR can infer the locations of satphones in various DCSNs within hundreds of meters in several minutes. Background and Motivation We begin by introducing the preliminaries of DCSNs. 2.1. Direct-to-Cell Satellite Networks (DCSN) Networking architecture of DCSNs. In general, direct-to- cell (DTC) satellites are communication satellites that can directly communicate to terrestrial satphones [2], [25], [26] without deploying extra dedicated dish-like antennas. DTC satellites, together with geo-distributed ground stations, can build a direct-to-cell satellite network (DCSN), providing not only telephony and short message services (SMS), but also broadband Internet access for terrestrial users. For example, Iridium is a DCSN which currently provides SMS and telephony services for about 2.4 million satphone customers around the world [27]. More recently in March to-cell services (known as Starlink DTC), which can achieve up to 17Mbps downlink speed for terrestrial users [28]. Depending on the functionality of satellites, 3GPP has defined two kinds of networking architecture for DCSNs [29] as depicted in Figure 1: (i) transparent mode, in which satellites lack on-board processing capabilities and simply forward packets between satphones and ground stations, such as changing the frequency carrier of the received uplink RF signal and amplifying it before transmitting on the downlink. Base station functions are offloaded to the ground; (ii) regenerative mode, in which satellites have on- board processing capabilities such as demodulation/decoding, switching/routing and modulation/coding, etc., enabling them to function as “flying base stations” in space. To enable DTC communication, three threads of protocols have been designed for current and upcoming DCSNs. • (i) GSM extensions. Since the 2G era, mobile network operators have extended the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) standard [30], [31] to adapt to satellite scenarios, and deployed DTC satellites ( e.g., Irid- ium [1], Inmarsat [32] and ViaSat [33]) to provide SMS and telephony services from space. These DCSNs require users to purchase a dedicated satphone different from normal cellphones.
